column3: A contrary face-and-mosque use: ritual orientation distinguishes these terms from 17:7's punitive turning and entry.
The ch005 route pairs rescue of some with force that reaches the culpable, clarifying the incursion's differentiated outcome.
A reversal of apparent superiority provides a counterpoint to the condemned elevation dismantled in 17:7.
The first enacted promise supplies the immediate precedent: severe force enters and searches the dwellings.
It states the prior corruption and great elevation that 17:7 brings to their later consequence.
The ch005-to-ch010 route and تَبَّرْنَا portray destruction as reduction to fragments, extending the dismantling reading.
Its face language concerns purification before prayer, only distinguishing a separate use of the shared term.
The ch005 threshold route offers a contrary, controlled entry scene ending in abasement of the proud.
Planned evil is turned away from one party and closes around its planners, sharpening evil's return upon its agents.
Its same latter promise places 17:7 within a later gathering of the addressed people.
The return of power, wealth, and numbers supplies the counterturn between the two promised incursions.
Its تَبَارًا route reinforces dismantling as the disintegration of an unjust order.
Its directional faces and mosque clarify a ritual use distinct from the forceful face and mosque clauses in 17:7.
It supplies the Moses and بني إسرائيل frame that precedes the sequence of corruption and return.
It gives a distinct asymmetry: good is multiplied while evil is limited to its like, refining the return-to-self reading.
Equity, faces, and mosque join orientation to accountable devotion, a secondary contrast to 17:7's terms.
Its ch005 and ch003 routes concern openings in bounded terrain, a remote structural parallel only.
It shows good answering evil with a transforming counteraction, extending the ethical side of self-directed action.
A true promise arriving reduces a constructed barrier to dust, closely paralleling decisive dismantling at the appointed time.
It completes the immediate cycle: renewed return is met by renewed consequence and enclosure.
It frames an established cult and its works as already destined for nullification, supporting the dismantling of entrenched order.
Their attribution of good to themselves and bad to others supplies a contrary model of how outcomes are misread.
Shared provision to both sides is a contextual qualification: present supply alone does not settle the later outcome.
Breach of commitment explicitly turns back upon one's own self, a narrower parallel to the focus's return principle.
It identifies mosques as exclusively God's, supplying a normative contrast to forced entry into the mosque in 17:7.
The ch005 route shows overwhelming force compelling a belated confession, a secondary outcome of decisive intervention.
It exposes visible dominance as a false measure of success, contrasting with the fate of those who elevate themselves.
The ch005 threshold route gives a protected, fear-free entry, contrasting with 17:7's coercive entry.
The opening passage between two mosques supplies a broader movement-and-sanctuary frame for the later mosque event.
The self's pull toward evil and mercy's restraint give an inward mechanism for action's return upon the self.
The appointed meeting and first creation supply an eschatological frame for the focus's final promise.
Its warning signs and ch008 link add only a general warning context, without the focus's return or dismantling pattern.
It joins restraint from wrong with active good, defining the ethical posture that the focus makes consequential.
What was amassed for selves becomes their own painful consequence, a concrete self-return pattern.
Noah's gratitude supplies only a distant positive example within the opening passage.
Regret after seeing the consequence shows that a wished-for return cannot reopen an already closed action cycle.
Its provision for selves gives only a broad future-facing ethical parallel.
The first-creation and nearness language offers a general return frame but no specific link to the focus's sequence.
Its repeated ihsan establishes a fitting correspondence between good and its return, complementing the focus's first clause.
Persistence in first rejection is followed by a reversal affecting the rejecters, a secondary action-consequence pattern.
The ch006 childbirth route does not add to either retained reading of 17:7.
It connects recognizing good with doing good and a later good outcome, adding a broad ethical continuation.
Solitary return and severed claimed supports add an accountability frame to the focus's personal consequence.
The adjacent guidance and reward for righteous action state the positive side of the passage's moral ordering.
As a contrast route, its exact recompense formulation tests a stricter correspondence than the focus's broader return pattern.
Wrongful obstruction and ruin of mosques contrast with 17:7's entry and destruction, distinguishing their moral setting.
Its parent context adds ordering and reckoning motifs but no distinct development of the focus.
Its practical superiority concerns timing and capacity, only a limited contrast to destructive elevation.
Broken pledges, expulsion, and an initiated first encounter add a secondary conflict-cycle parallel.
The ch006 route and gathering scene do not clarify either personal return or dismantling here.
The isolated goodness descriptor adds no distinct relation after the earlier ihsan readings.
Acceptance of the best deeds alongside passing over evil gives a distinct restorative form of moral consequence.
The next verse supplies the passage's negative eschatological consequence for those denying the latter reality.
As a contrast route, it keeps the possibility that public scheming rebounds on its makers without making it the preferred reading.
The arrival of an unpostponable term strengthens the finality of the focus's appointed promise.
Satanic promises and inducement offer only a diffuse contrary source of corrupting action.
The arrival of God's command adds timing but no further account of the focus's consequences.
Good expenditure is explicitly for selves, a concise parallel to the focus's first clause.
The b004 ch005-to-ch010 route makes destruction of deniers a direct parallel to the focus's dismantling action.
A general recompense formula corroborates good's return but adds little after the earlier specific accounts.
Good put forward for selves and later found with God gives a concrete positive-return formulation.
The adjacent warning that humans invoke evil as good qualifies the focus by showing moral misdirection and haste.
Its creation-and-provision sequence and divine uniqueness add no specific development of the focus.
Blocked mosque access and protected unknown believers complicate any simple reading of entry as an unqualified good.
Repeated examples met with flight add only a general resistance motif.
It repeats the earlier general recompense formula without a new angle.
It distinguishes righteousness from merely turning faces, clarifying that moral good exceeds external orientation.
Past communities' strength and monuments fail before their end, a secondary warning against durable elevation.
Its warning-to-wrongdoers and glad tidings-to-good-doers repeat the moral bifurcation without advancing it.
It directly joins refusal of elevation and corruption to the latter abode, sharply framing the focus's destructive target.
The repeated examples and rejection add only a general local context.
It repeats the already supplied general recompense formula.
Its promised succession, establishment, and safety under faithful worship provide a constructive counter-reading to corrupt elevation.
The ch003 route and isolated challenge do not clarify either focus reading.
Divine exaltation forms a clear contrast to the human elevation condemned in the focus.
The grant of scripture, judgment, and prophethood supplies only broad historical context.
God's transcendent elevation contrasts with the great elevation attributed to the corrupt actors in the opening sequence.
Its balanced request for near and latter good is only a broad echo of good's beneficial outcome.
No worker's deed is lost and wrongs are covered, adding an assurance of individualized moral outcome.
Just measure is a local ethical instruction but does not extend the focus's return or destruction pattern.
It repeats the earlier general recompense formula without a new angle.
Good in this life and uprightness in the latter life add a two-stage continuity of beneficial outcome.
Acknowledged self-wrong and forgiveness give a personal-return case tempered by mercy.
It identifies rising against God with domineering authority, sharply specifying the elevation that is opposed.
Good put forward for selves and found greater later reinforces the focus's beneficial return with delayed reward.
The impotence of alleged partners to remove harm gives only a remote theological contrast.
Striving and guided paths add a general positive trajectory after earlier fuller accounts of good's return.
The inheritance apportionments do not clarify either retained focus reading.
Its counsel of gentle speech belongs to a different local ethical setting.
Removal of past evil and recompense for best deeds restates the restorative dimension, with limited new detail after 46:16.
The fasting provisions do not add to the focus's moral-return or dismantling themes.
It forbids renewed corruption after repair and joins mercy to good action, integrating both focus readings.
Its separation of loyalties offers only a distant, qualified model for resolving hostile relations.
Self-purification is challenged by divine purification, qualifying any self-assessment within the return-to-self reading.
Its relational ethics and possible good in what is disliked are too remote from the focus.
No one bears another's burden, while purification benefits one's own self: a direct account of individual return.
Its complaint about alms distribution does not add to either focus reading.
Capacity-matched obligation, a truthful record, and no injustice specify how individualized consequence is judged.
Its instruction to accept peace is a separate conflict ethic without a focus-specific link.
Shared origin adds little to the already established account of individual moral return.
Its paired earning for and against the self is a direct formulation of the focus's personal-return pattern.
It places every good and evil deed before the person, adding an explicit scene of confronted consequence.
It distinguishes received good from evil traced to the self, a close parallel to the focus's asymmetrical clauses.
Acquiring sin upon one's own self gives a direct individual-accountability formulation.
The stated recompense for evil adds a general rule of consequence, though without the focus's historical sequence.
Covenant-breaking, curse, and hardened hearts supply an earlier Israelite pattern of collective moral consequence.
The destruction of earlier, more powerful generations provides a broad warning that established strength is not secure.
The cutting off of wrongdoers' root gives a concise image of total removal of a corrupt order.
Individual burden-bearing reinforces the personal limit on responsibility assumed by the focus's return-to-self statement.
Loss of selves at the scales gives an explicit judgment form for self-inflicted failure.
It explicitly destroys what Pharaoh and his people made and raised, closely specifying dismantling of elevated domination.
The punishment of wrongdoers after transgression adds a collective consequence pattern.
The announced continuing oppression of the transgressors extends the Israelite cycle of consequence.
Those who deny the signs are said to wrong themselves, directly naming self-directed harm.
It states that people wrong themselves rather than being wronged, a foundational parallel to the focus's first reading.
The prayer against Pharaoh's wealth and hardened dominance supplies a related anti-entrenchment scene.
Destroyed peoples are said to have wronged themselves, linking ruin to their own action.
The severe seizure of wrongdoing towns gives a general model for the focus's appointed intervention.
A people’s condition changes through what is within themselves, adding an inward collective mechanism of consequence.
Dwelling in the places of self-wronging peoples makes their prior end a warning within inhabited space.
Those struck by evil are said to have wronged themselves, restating consequence without external injustice.
The evil they acted upon encloses them, a direct return-of-action image.
A secure town's corruption turning into hunger and fear supplies a social counterturn from settled security.
Each person's attached record and its later presentation establish an explicit architecture of personal consequence.
The command to read one's record makes the self sufficient as witness for its own accounting.
Guidance benefits the guided self and error lies against it, directly matching the focus's bilateral return.
It states the sequence of a corrupt town's command, defiance, decisive word, and destruction.
Every town's pre-judgment destruction or punishment gives the focus's event a wider appointed-judgment frame.
Attempted expulsion from the land and the opponents' brief stay give a nearby displacement-and-counterturn parallel.
Moses' signs before Pharaoh add immediate Israelite historical context to the surrounding passage.
Pharaoh's attempted expulsion is reversed in his drowning, a direct counterturn within the same Israelite sequence.
Destroyed towns at their appointed term reinforce the focus's fixed-time intervention.
The calf is burned and scattered, a concrete dismantling of an elevated cultic object.
The destruction of wrongdoing towns gives a compact collective-judgment parallel.
Breaking the idols into fragments supplies a precise material analogue for تَتْبِيرًا.
Overthrown towns and abandoned structures make visible the material aftermath of corrupt rule.
The destruction of a sign-denying people introduces the warning before the already listed fragmentation scene.
The end of plotting is the destruction of plotters and their people, joining rebound with collective ruin.
Pharaoh's self-exaltation, social division, and weakening of a people sharply frame the elevation opposed in 17:7.
The destruction of prosperous towns warns that inhabited abundance cannot secure an unjust settlement.
Qarun's swallowing with his dwelling gives a material collapse of accumulated, elevated power.
Each community is seized for its sin, and the verse explicitly denies that they were wronged rather than self-wronging.
The fate of earlier peoples is attributed to their wronging of themselves despite their greater earthly strength.
Disbelief lies against its agent while righteous action is prepared for the agents themselves, directly paralleling both focus clauses.
The grateful or ungrateful response to a settled land offers a constructive counterpoint to social collapse.
The reversal of a flourishing settlement after refusal gives a clear societal counterturn.
Scattering a people into fragments supplies a distinct image of dismantled communal order.
The destruction of earlier generations and their non-return provides a terse finality motif.
Responsibility for disbelief and the rule that no bearer carries another's burden reinforce individual accountability.
Earlier powers with greater strength are seized for their sins, a close warning against entrenched might.
Its exact pairing of righteous action for oneself and evil against oneself is the closest verbal parallel to the focus's first half.
Affliction through what hands have earned, with much pardoned, adds a calibrated account of consequence and mercy.
Blame upon those who wrong and transgress on earth identifies the agents to whom adverse consequence belongs.
Its exact bilateral formulation of good for oneself and evil against oneself directly restates the focus's moral logic.
The destruction of surrounding towns after repeated signs adds a warning-before-ruin pattern.
Travel through the earth to see destroyed predecessors ties rejection to the collapse of prior orders.
Expulsion and the ruin of houses by their own and others' hands give a close dwelling-and-destruction parallel.
A town’s strict accounting supplies an explicit reckoning stage before its disastrous consequence.
Tasting the consequence of its affair and ending in loss gives a compact collective-return formula.
The overwhelming wind against ʿĀd supplies a historical example of force undoing a powerful people.
Bodies left as hollow remnants makes the material aftermath of that undoing explicit.
Sins preceding drowning and fire tightly join wrongful action to catastrophic consequence.
Pharaoh's claim to be the highest gives a stark contrary instance of the elevation condemned in the focus.
Pharaoh's exemplary punishment supplies the consequence paired with his claim of highestness.
It identifies earlier powerful peoples as those who spread corruption in the lands, directly matching the focus's precondition.
The poured scourge upon those corrupters gives the punitive counterpart to their elevated corruption.
Purification's success supplies the constructive personal counterpart to self-inflicted loss.
The failure of corrupting the self gives the negative inward counterpart to the focus's first clause.
Thamud's sin is followed by their leveling, joining transgression to literal destruction.
Seeing even an atom's weight of good supplies the smallest-scale confirmation of good's return.
Seeing even an atom's weight of evil supplies the smallest-scale confirmation of evil's return.
